1.open: When did you last feel completely overwhelmed by something bigger than you, like a view, a storm, or a piece of news?
questions: Verse 3 says, "Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy." This book was first heard together out loud, not read alone. What changes when you hear a passage with other people instead of reading it by yourself?
Jesus is called "the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth" (v. 5). Why might those words matter to people living under Roman power?
John describes Jesus as the one "who loves us and has released us from our sins by His blood" (v. 5). How does it feel to hear that love named before anything else in the book?

John calls himself "your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus" (v. 9). Why might it matter that he writes as a fellow sufferer and not from a distance?
Verse 17 says, "I fell at His feet like a dead man." What do you make of John's reaction? Where, if anywhere, have you felt awe or fear in front of God, and where have you felt nothing at all?

Jesus answers John with "Do not be afraid" and then points to himself: "I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever!" (vv. 17, 18). Why do you think he answers fear with who he is and not with an explanation?

The picture in verses 12 to 16 is full of symbols, and Jesus stands "among the lampstands," which verse 20 says are the churches. What does it say to you that he is in the middle of his people and not far off?
Verses 1 and 3 say the time is near, and Christians read this book in different ways. What would you honestly like to ask about it, or what makes you hesitate to open it?
1.life: Verse 18 says Jesus holds "the keys of Death and of Hades." This week, name one fear that feels too big for you, and each time it comes up, quietly remind yourself in your own words that Jesus is alive and holds the keys.
1.prayer: Thank Jesus that he is "the First and the Last," "the Living One" (vv. 17, 18). Ask him to meet each person in the group in whatever they fear right now, and to help you listen to this book together.
1.tip: Revelation's images can pull the group into guessing about timelines and symbols. Say early that Christians read this book in different ways, then steer back to what the chapter plainly shows: Jesus is alive, present with his people, and tells them not to be afraid.

2.open: Think of a hobby, friendship or job you were once really excited about. What did that early excitement look like?
questions: Jesus praises Ephesus for hard work and for the fact that "without growing weary, you have persevered" (v. 3). What kinds of faithful effort do you see in your own church or home group that deserve that kind of thanks?
Then comes the hard line: "You have abandoned your first love" (v. 4). What do you think that looked like in a church that was still working so hard? What might it look like in a person?

Jesus says, "keep in mind how far you have fallen. Repent and perform the deeds you did at first" (v. 5). What is one small thing that helped your faith feel alive and close to God at some point, and what would it take to come back to it?

To poor and persecuted Smyrna he says, "Do not fear what you are about to suffer" (v. 10). What do you think it meant for them to hear that? What fear would you most like Jesus to speak to in your life?

Pergamum held on bravely, yet some also followed teaching that mixed in idol feasts and sexual sin (vv. 13-14). Where do believers today feel pressure to blend in with the surrounding culture, and how can we tell a harmless custom from a real compromise?

Thyatira was growing in love, faith, service and perseverance, yet it tolerated a false teacher (vv. 19-20). Why might a loving church find it hard to say no? Is there a difference between being gracious and tolerating harm?

Each letter ends with a promise to "the one who overcomes," such as the tree of life and a new name (vv. 7, 17). Which promise speaks to you most right now, and which one feels hard to believe or hard to understand? Be as honest as you like.

The letters are blunt, yet Jesus begins each with "I know" (vv. 2, 9, 13, 19). How does it change the way you hear correction to know that the one speaking sees everything about you and still writes to the church?
2.life: Pick one thing that once helped you love God, such as a kind of prayer, a song, a walk, time with a certain friend, or reading a Gospel slowly. Make room for it two or three times this week, and notice what happens in you.
2.prayer: Ask Jesus to show each of you where love has gone quiet beneath busyness or habit. Pray for the courage to turn back, and for anyone in the group who is afraid or worn out.
2.tip: Some will stumble over the harsh images, such as "synagogue of Satan" (v. 9) or the threats against Jezebel and her children (vv. 22-23). Say plainly that these refer to specific first-century disputes and are never a license to condemn any group of people today. Then steer back to the main point: Jesus corrects the churches because he loves them and walks among them (v. 1). If time is short, focus on Ephesus and Smyrna.

3.open: Think of a time you were sure everything was fine, whether with a car, a house or a plan, and it turned out it wasn't. What happened?
questions: Sardis had "a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead" (v. 1). Why do you think a church, or a person, can look healthy from the outside and be struggling underneath?
Jesus says, "Wake up and strengthen what remains" (v. 2). He does not say to start over. What might it look like for a church or a person to strengthen what is left?
In verse 3 Jesus says, "Remember, then, what you have received and heard." What from your faith story, a person, a moment or a verse, is worth remembering when things feel flat?
Philadelphia had "only a little strength, yet you have kept My word" (v. 8). Jesus has no rebuke for them. What do you make of that, and how does it sit with how you see your own strength?

Verse 10 speaks of being kept "from the hour of testing." Some Christians read this as being taken away before a time of suffering, and many read it as being kept safe through it. Whichever way you lean, what does the promise say about how God treats people who stay faithful?

Laodicea says, "I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing," but Jesus calls them "wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked" (v. 17). Where is it easy to feel self-sufficient today, and what might we be missing?
Verse 19 says, "Those I love I rebuke and discipline." How does it feel to hear hard words and love in the same sentence? Has anyone ever corrected you in a way that turned out to be care?
Jesus says, "I stand at the door and knock" (v. 20). If you are honest, are you more likely to hear that knock right now as comfort, as challenge, or as something you are not sure about? Why?
3.life: Pick one ordinary moment this week, like a meal, and treat it as a chance to make room for Jesus. Say a simple line in your own words, inviting him to join you. Notice what, if anything, changes.
3.prayer: Ask God to show you honestly where you are asleep, tired or self-satisfied, without shame. Thank him that he knocks and keeps knocking out of love.
3.tip: Verse 9 has a painful history, because lines like it have been twisted to fuel hatred of Jewish people. Explain briefly that it most likely describes a local dispute in one first century city, that most churches today firmly reject any anti-Jewish use of it, and then return to the three main letters. Also note that verse 20 is often used as an invitation to individuals, but it was first spoken to a church.

4.open: What is the most impressive place you have ever walked into, and how did it make you feel?
questions: John is told, "Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things" (v. 1). Why do you think God shows John heaven before he shows him anything about the earth?

The first thing John sees is "a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it" (v. 2). What does it mean to you that the center of everything is a throne with someone on it, and not chaos or an empty seat?
John describes God only through light and gemstones, "like jasper and carnelian" (v. 3), and never gives a face or a body. Why might he describe God this way?

The four living creatures say day and night, "Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!" (v. 8). What does the word holy bring to your mind, and does it feel comforting, frightening, or something else?

The elders "cast their crowns before the throne" (v. 10). What do people in our day hold onto most tightly, like status, achievements, or control, and what would it look like to lay one of those down?

The elders praise God because "You created all things; by Your will they exist and were created" (v. 11). How does seeing God as Creator change the way you look at your own life or at the world around you?

John's first readers lived under an empire that demanded loyalty and honor. What might this scene have said to people who felt small and powerless? What might it say to us when life feels out of control?

This scene is full of awe, and some people find it moving while others find it distant or hard to relate to. Where are you honestly at with worship right now, and what would help you feel closer to God?
4.life: Each day this week, take two quiet minutes to picture the throne room and say, "Worthy are You, our Lord and God" (v. 11). Then name one thing you are holding tightly and hand it over to God in your own words.
4.prayer: Praise God as holy and as Creator of all things. Ask for a heart that is willing to set down its own crowns, and pray for anyone in the group who feels small or out of control right now.
4.tip: Revelation 4 has a lot of strange symbols, and the group may get pulled into debating who the twenty-four elders are or when these events happen. Christians read these details differently, including whether verse 1 pictures the church being taken to heaven. Say that plainly once, then bring everyone back to what all readers agree on: God is on the throne and worthy of worship.

5.open: Think of a time you were waiting on news or an answer that you couldn't control. What was that like?
questions: John sees a scroll that no one is able to open, and he "began to weep bitterly" (v. 4). Why do you think this moved him so deeply? When have you felt that something important was out of reach?
An elder says, "Do not weep!" and points John to "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (v. 5). What does a lion make you think of, and what kind of rescuer would you expect from that name?
John turns and sees "a Lamb who appeared to have been slain," yet standing (v. 6). Why do you think the chapter gives us a lion in words and a lamb in the picture?
The song says, "Worthy are You" because "You were slain" (v. 9). What does this chapter suggest makes someone worthy to hold power? How does that compare with how the world usually decides?

The golden bowls are "the prayers of the saints" (v. 8). Christians read this a little differently, but all agree that prayers matter to God. What would it mean for you that your prayers are treasured and not lost?
The Lamb bought people "from every tribe and tongue and people and nation" (v. 9). Who is hardest for you to picture in that crowd, and what might that say about your own heart or habits?
The song says they are made "a kingdom and priests to serve our God" (v. 10). What do you think it looks like for ordinary people to live that way on a Monday?

Every creature joins the praise (v. 13), but in real life many of us find worship dry or find faith hard. Where are you right now: singing along, standing quietly at the edge, or full of questions? What would you say honestly?
5.life: Each day this week, name one situation that feels locked or out of your control, and hand it to Jesus in a sentence of prayer. Then write down one way you saw him at work, even a small one, to share next time.
5.prayer: Thank Jesus that he is worthy and that he is the Lamb who was slain. Ask him to calm the fears the group is carrying and to help each person trust him with what they cannot open themselves.
5.tip: Revelation 5 sits inside a book Christians read in very different ways, and the group may drift into arguing about what the scroll holds or when its events happen. Say in one line that Christians disagree on that, then steer back to what everyone can see in this chapter: Jesus is the Lamb, he is worthy, and all creation worships him.

6.open: When you were a kid, what was the scariest thing you ever watched or heard about, and how did you get through it?
questions: Each time, it is the Lamb who opens the seal (vv. 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 12). Why might John want us to see that the one who was slain is the one holding the scroll?

The first rider "was given a crown, and he rode out to overcome and conquer" (v. 2). Christians disagree on whether this is Christ or a conquering power. What leads you toward one reading or the other?
The riders bring war, hunger and death (vv. 4, 6, 8). Which of these feels closest to the world you see in the news, or in your own street?

The black horse brings famine, while the voice says "do not harm the oil and wine" (v. 6). Why do you think some people go hungry while others keep their comforts, and what do you make of that picture?
The souls under the altar cry, "How long, O Lord, holy and true" (v. 10). Is there a "how long?" you have been carrying lately? How would you say it to God, honestly and in your own words?
The martyrs are given "a white robe" and told "to rest a little while longer" (v. 11). What do you hear in that answer: comfort, frustration, or something else? Be honest about it.
In verses 15 to 17 everyone from kings to slaves hides from "the wrath of the Lamb." Why might John put wrath and the Lamb side by side? How do you feel about God's anger at wrong?
The chapter ends with the question, "who is able to withstand it?" (v. 17). What does the question stir up in you, and where do you look for an answer?
6.life: Revelation 6 gives voice to the cry "How long?" This week, name one hurt or injustice, in your life or in the world, and bring it to God in plain words. Then do one small thing for someone who is hungry, grieving or treated unfairly.
6.prayer: Thank God that the Lamb holds the scroll and that no suffering goes unseen. Bring your own "how long?" to him, and pray for people who are hungry, afraid or wronged.
6.tip: This chapter can frighten people and invite heated arguments about timing. Say up front that Christians read the seals differently: events in John's own day, patterns that repeat through history, or a future time before Christ returns. Then keep the group on what is clear: the Lamb is in charge, God hears the cry of the wronged, and evil does not get the last word.

7.open: Think of a time you were in a huge crowd, like a stadium, a wedding or a festival. What do you remember about it?
questions: In verses 1 to 3 the winds are held back until God's servants are sealed. What do you think it means to be marked as belonging to God, and how does that picture land with you?
John hears "144,000 from all the tribes of Israel" (v. 4). What do you notice about how the list is put together, and why might John want us to hear it as a complete and counted people?

Christians read the 144,000 differently. Some see a symbol of all God's people, and others see a literal group of Jewish believers. How do you hear it, and what do you think is at stake in the question?

Then John sees "a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue" (v. 9). Who is in your church or community that you would not have expected to be in that crowd, and how would it change things if they were standing beside you?

The crowd cries, "Salvation to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" (v. 10). They give the credit for their rescue to God. Why might it matter that they praise instead of celebrating their own endurance?

The elder says they "have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (v. 14). Blood making something white sounds odd. What do you think the picture is saying about how we are made clean?

Verse 14 speaks of those who "have come out of the great tribulation." Some think of a future time and others of suffering in every age. Either way, what do you do with the fact that this vision does not skip over pain?

Verse 17 says "God will wipe away every tear from their eyes." What tears are you carrying right now, or have carried, and what do you honestly make of this promise? It is fine to say you find it hard to believe.
7.life: Pick one person who is going through something hard. This week, reach out with a call, a meal or a visit, and simply stay with them without trying to fix it. Let the picture of the Shepherd who wipes away tears shape how you show up.
7.prayer: Thank God that his people are known, marked and counted, and that the crowd around his throne includes every nation. Name before him the people and the sorrows you are carrying, and ask for his comfort.
7.tip: The 144,000 can swallow the whole evening, and people hold their views strongly. Say plainly in one line that Christians read it differently, then steer to verses 9 to 17, where the comfort is clearest. Also watch verse 17: someone in the group may be grieving, so let silence and honest doubt be welcome rather than rushing to reassure.

8.open: When did you last sit in a silence that felt important, like a pause before big news, a hush at a gathering, or a quiet moment outdoors?
questions: Verse 1 says "there was silence in heaven for about half an hour." Why do you think John tells us about the quiet? What do you imagine it was like?
Verse 3 says the incense was offered "along with the prayers of all the saints." What does it mean to you that God's people's prayers are gathered up and brought before him?
John was writing to Christians who were under pressure and sometimes suffering for their faith. Why might a picture of their prayers rising before God have mattered to them?
Verse 4 says the smoke and prayers "rose up before God." Think of a prayer you have prayed for a long time with no clear answer. What do you do with that waiting?

In verse 5 the same censer is filled with fire from the altar and thrown down to the earth. Many readers link this to believers crying out for justice. When you have wanted a wrong put right, what did you really hope would happen?
Each of the first four trumpets strikes "a third" of something (vv. 7-12). What do you make of the limit, and what might it say about how God deals with a broken world?
Verse 11 says "many people died from the bitter waters." These verses are hard to read. If you feel unsettled or unsure what to make of them, what part troubles you most?
The eagle cries "Woe! Woe! Woe" as a warning that worse is coming (v. 13). Why might God warn before the final trumpets sound, and what does a warning tell us about him?
8.life: Choose one prayer you have been carrying for a long time, for a person, a hurt or a situation. Write it down and pray it each day this week, trusting that it is not lost but held before God.
8.prayer: Thank God that he hears the prayers of his people and does not let them go unnoticed. Ask for patience in waiting, and pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a long, unanswered request.
8.tip: The trumpets raise many questions about timing and meaning, and Christians read them in four main ways: events in the first century, a timeline of later history, disasters still to come, or symbolic pictures of judgment across all history. Say this early and plainly, then steer the group back to what is clear: God hears prayer, judgment is held in limits, and a warning comes first. Don't try to settle which reading is right, and be gentle with anyone who finds the harm in these verses upsetting.

9.open: What is something you kept putting off even after you knew you should deal with it?
questions: The chapter opens with a star that is given "the key to the pit of the Abyss" (v. 1). The key is given, not taken. What does it say that even this dark scene happens under limits someone else sets?

The locusts are told not to harm the plants, "but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads" (v. 4). Why might John want his readers to know that God marks and protects his people?
Verse 6 says people "will long to die, but death will escape them." How do you react to such a harsh picture? Say honestly what it stirs in you, even if it is discomfort or doubt.
The locusts and the army are strange mixtures of horses, scorpions, lions and men (vv. 7-10). Why do you think John uses such wild images instead of plain description? What do they make you feel?
A third of mankind is killed (v. 18), and the text presents it as allowed by God. How do you hold that alongside what you know of God's mercy? What questions does it raise for you?

Christians read this chapter differently. Some see future events, some see John's own day, and some see symbols of evil and judgment that repeat in every age. What do you take from the chapter whichever reading you lean toward?
Verse 20 says the survivors "still did not repent of the works of their hands." Why do you think suffering changes some people and only hardens others?

Verses 20 and 21 describe people holding on to idols, "murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft." Where do you see people, or yourself, clinging to something that cannot help? What might it take to let go?
9.life: Revelation 9 shows people who would not turn even when things fell apart. This week, think of one habit or comfort you keep returning to in place of God. Name it honestly to him, and take one small step toward turning from it.
9.prayer: Thank God that he marks and protects his people. Ask for a soft heart that listens when he calls, and pray for someone you know who is hurting or hardened.
9.tip: This chapter is vivid and some people will be unsettled or tempted to debate timelines. Say early that Christians read it in several ways, and steer the group back to what is plain: God is in charge, his people are sealed, and the survivors still refuse to repent. Leave room for honest unease.

10.open: Have you ever been told to wait for something and found the waiting harder than you expected? What was it?
questions: John sees an angel "wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head" (v. 1). What do you notice about this picture, and what feeling does it give you about God's power?

The angel has one foot "on the sea" and the other "on the land" (v. 2). What do you think that image says about who is in charge of the world? Some readers see Christ in this figure and others see a great angel. How does the text itself describe him?

When the seven thunders speak, John is told, "Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down" (v. 4). Why might God keep some things hidden? How do you feel about not getting every answer?
The angel swears, "There will be no more delay!" (v. 6). Many of us feel that God is slow. If you are willing, tell about a time you wondered whether God was ever going to act.
Verse 7 says "the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets." What does it mean to you that God's plan was announced long ago and will be finished?
John is told the scroll will be "as sweet as honey" in his mouth but make his stomach bitter (v. 9). Can you think of a truth from God that was sweet to hear and also hard to take in?
John is told, "You must prophesy again" (v. 11). Why do you think he is sent out again after such a strange experience? Where might you feel a nudge to keep going when you would rather rest?
Christians read Revelation in different ways, and that is okay. What helps you keep reading a book like this with hope instead of fear or confusion?
10.life: Pick one thing you are waiting on God for. Each day this week, say out loud that God is the one who "lives forever and ever" (v. 6), and tell him honestly how the waiting feels, sweet or bitter or both.
10.prayer: Thank God that he made everything and keeps his promises. Ask for patience in the waiting, and for trust in the things he has not told us.
10.tip: The seven thunders and the timing of the oath can pull the group into guessing about the future. Say kindly that the text keeps the thunders secret, name that Christians read Revelation in different ways, and bring people back to what is clear: God is in charge, his plan will be finished, and his word is both sweet and costly.

11.open: Think of a time you were the bearer of news people did not want to hear. How did it go?
questions: John is told to measure "the temple of God and the altar, and count the number of worshipers there" (v. 1). Many read this as God marking his people as his own even while they suffer on the outside. What does it mean to you that God knows and counts his people?
The witnesses prophesy "clothed in sackcloth" (v. 3), the rough cloth people wore when they were grieving. Why might a message from God come with sorrow rather than swagger?

Christians read the two witnesses differently: two real prophets near the end of history, or the faithful church bearing witness in every age. Which reading makes more sense to you, and what would change in how you live either way?

When the witnesses finish their testimony, they are overpowered and killed, and people "send one another gifts" because the prophets had tormented them (vv. 7-10). Why do you think the truth can feel like torment to some people?

Their bodies lie in the street, and then "the breath of life from God entered" them and they stand on their feet (v. 11). What does this picture say about who has the last word, and where do you most need to hear that?

After the earthquake, the survivors "were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven" (v. 13). Some read that as real repentance and others as fear alone. What do you think draws a person toward God: fear, kindness, or something else?

The voices in heaven say, "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ" (v. 15). Looking at the news or your own life right now, what is it like to trust that statement, and what makes it hard? It is fine to answer honestly if you are unsure.
The elders thank God because he has taken his great power and begun to reign (v. 17). What is one area of your life or our world where you would like to see his rule more clearly?
11.life: Pick one situation this week where you feel pressure to stay quiet about what is true or kind or faithful. Ask God for wisdom about how and whether to speak, and then read verse 15 aloud before you go in.
11.prayer: Thank God that he will reign forever and ever. Ask for faithfulness and gentleness for anyone in the group who feels worn down for doing what is right.
11.tip: Revelation 11 is one of the most debated chapters in the Bible, and the group may get stuck on who the two witnesses are or what the 42 months mean. Say early that faithful Christians read it differently, then steer back to what everyone can agree on: God's people bear witness, suffering is not the end, and God reigns.

12.open: Think of a story, movie or fairy tale with a great villain. What made that villain memorable?
questions: John calls the first scene "a great sign" (v. 1). Signs point beyond themselves. How does it change your reading to treat the woman and the dragon as pictures rather than a map of events?

Christians read the woman differently: Catholic tradition especially sees Mary, many Protestants see God's people, Israel and then the church, and many see more than one layer. What might we gain from hearing more than one reading?
The dragon stands "ready to devour her child" (v. 4). Think of Pharaoh and Herod, who both went after baby boys. What does this picture say about how evil treats God's rescue plan?
God had "prepared a place for her to be nourished" in the wilderness (v. 6). When have you felt like you were in a wilderness, and what, if anything, kept you going?
The loud voice calls the devil "the accuser of our brothers" and says he "has been thrown down" (v. 10). What accusing thoughts do you hear most often, and how might this verse speak to them?
Verse 11 says they conquered "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony." Nobody swings a sword. What surprises you about how this victory is won?

Verse 12 says the devil knows "he has only a short time," and verse 17 says he goes after those who "keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus." How do you make sense of a victory that has been won while things still hurt?

What do you think people gain, and what might they lose, by picturing their struggles as part of a bigger battle between good and evil? If this chapter feels distant or hard to believe, what would you honestly say about it?
12.life: This week, when an accusing thought shows up, name it, then answer it out loud with verse 11 and what Jesus has done for you. Tell one person in the group how it went.
12.prayer: Thank God that the accuser has been thrown down and that Jesus has won. Ask for steady faith for anyone in the group who feels worn down or under attack.
12.tip: This chapter can pull a group into debates about timelines, the 1,260 days and exactly who the woman is. Say once, kindly, that Christians disagree on these, then steer back to the main point: the dragon is real and fierce, but he is defeated, and God's people are cared for.

13.open: Think of a trend, gadget or fashion that everyone seemed to follow at some point. Did you go along with it, and why?
questions: John says that after the beast's wound was healed, "the whole world marveled and followed the beast" (v. 3). What draws people to follow a powerful leader or system, even when something feels off?
The crowd asks, "Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?" (v. 4). The question is a twisted echo of praise for God. Where do you see power treated as if it deserved worship today?
The beast is "permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them" (v. 7), but only for "42 months" (v. 5). What does it mean that evil is real here but also limited?

Verse 8 speaks of names written in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb. If you are not sure you feel secure in God, what do you make of a book that is about the Lamb's care rather than our performance?
The second beast has "two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon" (v. 11). What does it look like when something appears gentle or religious but leads people away from God?

Verse 17 says "no one could buy or sell unless he had the mark." Early believers may have faced losing income if they refused to join in pagan worship. Where might loyalty to Jesus cost people something in work, money or reputation today?

Verse 10 calls for "the perseverance and faith of the saints." Translations differ on the exact wording of the verse, but the call to hold on is clear. What helps you keep going when faith is costly or tiring?
Verse 18 says, "Here is a call for wisdom." Many people have been tempted to treat 666 as a code to crack. How could our group read this chapter with wisdom instead of fear or speculation?
13.life: This week, notice one place where you feel pressure to give your loyalty, time or trust to something other than God, such as a leader, a brand, an image or a feed. Name it honestly in prayer, and take one small step to put Christ first there.
13.prayer: Thank God that the Lamb has the final word and that evil only has limited time. Ask for steady faith and clear thinking, and pray for believers around the world who pay a real price for following Jesus.
13.tip: This chapter can pull a group into debates about who the beast is and what 666 means. Say up front that Christians read these symbols differently (the Roman Empire of John's day, powers in every age, or a ruler still to come), and that nobody has to settle it tonight. Keep bringing people back to what all readings share: do not give worship to anyone but God, and hold on, because the Lamb wins.

14.open: Has there ever been a time when you were the only one in a room who didn't go along with something? What was that like?
questions: John sees the Lamb standing with people who have "His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads" (v. 1). What do you think it means to belong to God so openly that it is written on you?
Verse 4 says these people "follow the Lamb wherever He goes." What does following Jesus look like on an ordinary Tuesday, not just in dramatic moments?
Verse 5 says "no lie was found in their mouths." Why might honesty be one of the first things to suffer when we feel pressure to fit in?
An angel carries "the eternal gospel" to "every nation and tribe and tongue and people" (v. 6). What does it say about God's heart that good news goes out to everyone before judgment is described?

Verses 9 to 11 are a severe warning, and Christians understand the punishment differently, some as endless suffering and some as final destruction. How do you feel when you read this passage, and what do you want to ask God about it?
Verse 12 calls for "the perseverance of the saints." Where do you feel worn down right now, and what helps you keep going?
Verse 13 says those who die in the Lord "will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them." What comfort, or what questions, does that bring up for you?

The chapter ends with harvest pictures, one of grain and one of grapes in a winepress (vv. 14-20). Why might John show both the Lamb's people and the judgment of evil in the same chapter? What does that tell us about God?
14.life: Pick one small place this week where you are tempted to shade the truth or just go along with the crowd. Choose to be honest or to stand apart there, and ask Jesus for help beforehand.
14.prayer: Thank Jesus, the Lamb, that he leads his people and that they are known by his name. Ask for the strength to keep going and for hearts that care about those who do not yet know him.
14.tip: Verses 9 to 11 and 17 to 20 are intense, and people may be troubled or want to debate who is included. Say plainly that Christians disagree about how to read this imagery, including whether it points to the future or to John's own day. Then bring the group back to verse 12 and to the good news in verse 6, and let anyone who is unsettled say so without being corrected.

15.open: Think of a time when something unfair was finally put right, for you or for someone you know. How did it feel?
questions: John calls what he sees "another great and marvelous sign in heaven" (v. 1). The seven angels carry the last plagues, "with which the wrath of God is completed." What is your first reaction to a chapter that begins this way?
Those beside the glassy sea are "those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name" (v. 2). What do you think it meant for them to conquer? What did it likely cost them?

They sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb, like Israel singing after the Red Sea (v. 3). Why might a song be the right response to being rescued? When has singing or music helped you through something hard?

The song says, "Great and wonderful are Your works, O Lord God Almighty! Just and true are Your ways" (v. 3). Where in the world do you most want to see God's justice? What makes it hard to say these words today?
Verse 4 says, "All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed." What does it tell us that the song ends with all nations and not only a rescued few?

Verse 7 speaks of "seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God." Some people find God's anger hard to square with his love. If that is true for you, what troubles you most? Honest answers are welcome here.

Verse 8 says "no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed." The text does not say why. What do you make of that silence, and what does the scene say about God's glory and power?
15.life: Pick one case of cruelty or injustice you know about, in the news or close to home. Each day this week, pray the words of verse 3 over it: God's ways are just and true. If you notice a wish for revenge creeping in, hand it to God and ask him to be the one who sets things right.
15.prayer: Praise God that his ways are "just and true" (v. 3). Pray for people who are suffering under cruelty right now, and ask God to keep your longing for justice free of bitterness.
15.tip: Expect two hard spots: God's wrath, and what the plagues refer to. Christians differ on whether they point to the first century, church history, the future end of the world, or God's judgment on evil in every age. Say that in one line, then bring the group back to the song in verses 3 and 4. Let honest discomfort about wrath be spoken without rushing to fix it.

16.open: When something goes wrong at home, like a leak or a power cut, what is the first thing you usually do?
questions: The angels pour out bowls on the earth, the sea and the rivers (vv. 2-4). Many readers hear echoes of the plagues on Egypt in Exodus. What does that connection tell us about the kind of God this chapter shows?

The angel of the waters says, "Righteous are You, O Holy One, who is and was" (v. 5), and the altar answers, "true and just are Your judgments" (v. 7). Why might John want us to hear these voices of praise in the middle of such hard scenes?
Verse 6 ties the judgment to those who "spilled the blood of saints and prophets." Why might it matter to people who have suffered unjustly that God sees and answers? How does that sit with you?
Twice we read that people "did not repent" and that they cursed God for their pain (vv. 9, 11). What do you make of that? Why might hardship make some hearts softer and others harder?
Verse 15 breaks in with, "Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed." What does being ready look like in an ordinary week, without it turning into fear?

Christians read this chapter in different ways: as events of Rome's time, as events across history, as events still to come, or as pictures of judgment on oppressive powers in every age. How does the main message, that God will not leave evil unanswered, hold up under any of these readings?

At the end God's voice declares, "It is done!" (v. 17). When you read a chapter this heavy, what do you honestly feel, whether that is hope, fear, discomfort or doubt? What would you want to ask God about it?
16.life: This week, think of one person or place in the world suffering under injustice. Pray for them by name each day, and ask God what, if anything, you could do to help.
16.prayer: Thank God that he is just and that he sees every wrong. Ask him to keep your heart soft and awake, and to bring comfort to anyone who is suffering unjustly.
16.tip: This chapter is intense and people may be unsettled, or want to debate end-times timelines and Armageddon. Say plainly that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what all can share: God is just, evil does not have the last word, and we are called to stay ready. Leave room for anyone who finds the judgment hard to sit with.

17.open: What is something that looked impressive from the outside but turned out to be very different up close?
questions: John sees a woman dressed in "purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls" (v. 4). What does this picture make you feel, and why do you think John was shown her this way?

Her golden cup is "full of abominations" (v. 4), and the kings and the people are "intoxicated" by her (v. 2). What are some ways wealth, power or status can pull people in so that they stop asking hard questions?
The woman is "drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses for Jesus" (v. 6). What would it have meant for the first readers, many of them facing pressure and threats, to hear this?
John says he was "utterly amazed" at the sight of her (v. 6), and the angel asks, "Why are you so amazed?" (v. 7). When have you been dazzled by something and later seen it more clearly?

The angel says, "This calls for a mind with wisdom" (v. 9). The seven hills, seven kings and ten horns are confusing, and scholars do not agree on all of them. How do you usually handle parts of the Bible that feel puzzling, and what can you still take from this chapter?

The ten kings "will make war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will triumph over them" (v. 14). How does knowing how the story ends change the way you look at powerful forces that seem unstoppable today?

The angel says the "great city" rules "over the kings of the earth" (v. 18), yet her own allies turn on her (v. 16). What do you make of the idea that systems built on greed and violence eventually collapse? If parts of this chapter are hard for you to read or believe, what are they?
17.life: This week, notice one place where wealth, status or power is being made to look glamorous, whether in an ad, a show, your workplace or your own wishes. Ask yourself who might be paying the price, and bring that to God in prayer.
17.prayer: Thank God that the Lamb is "Lord of lords and King of kings" and that his people are called, chosen and faithful. Ask for clear eyes to see through what dazzles us, and pray for Christians who face pressure for their faith.
17.tip: Revelation 17 tempts a group to spend the whole time decoding the kings and the identity of Babylon. Name early that Christians read these symbols differently, then steer back to what is clear: the Lamb wins, and power built on greed and violence does not last. Also be gentle with the violent imagery in verse 16, since some will find it hard, and it is fine to say so.

18.open: What is something you once owned or loved that you were sure would last, but didn't?
questions: The angel cries, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!" (v. 2). John's first readers likely heard this as a message about the powerful empire around them. Why might that have been good news for people who felt small and unprotected?
Verse 3 says "the merchants of the earth have grown wealthy from the extravagance of her luxury." What does the chapter suggest about how wealth, power and desire can feed each other?

A voice says, "Come out of her, My people, so that you will not share in her sins" (v. 4). Readers differ on whether this means leaving physically or refusing her ways. What would it look like today to live in a place without taking on its values?
In verse 7 she says, "I sit as queen; I am not a widow and will never see grief." When have you seen confidence in success or security turn out to be fragile?
The merchants mourn because "there is no one left to buy their cargo" (v. 11). What do you notice about what they are sad about, and what they do not seem sad about?
The long list of goods ends with "bodies and souls of slaves" (v. 13). Why do you think the list ends there, and where might people still be treated as goods today?
Verse 20 says, "Rejoice over her, O heaven." Many readers find this hard. How do you feel about rejoicing at judgment, and what might it mean for people who have suffered injustice?
Be honest: do you find this chapter comforting, troubling, confusing, or something else? What would you want to ask God about it?
18.life: This week, pick one thing you buy or use often, like clothes, food or a phone, and find out a little about who makes it and under what conditions. Then talk to God about what, if anything, he is asking you to do with what you learn.
18.prayer: Thank God that no empire, however proud, has the last word. Ask him to show you where you are comfortable at someone else's cost, and to give you courage to live differently.
18.tip: People may jump straight to naming who Babylon is, and Christians disagree. Say so briefly, then steer back to what the chapter shows about pride, wealth and harm. Also, verse 20 can feel cold, so let people say that honestly rather than rushing to explain it away.

19.open: Think of a celebration you have been to, like a wedding, a homecoming or a big win. What do you remember most about it?
questions: The chapter opens with a huge crowd shouting, "Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!" (v. 1). Why do you think they are celebrating, and when was the last time you felt like celebrating over something God had done?

The crowd says God's judgments are "true and just" because the city had spilled "the blood of His servants" (v. 2). The note for this chapter says most scholars think the city pictures Rome. Why might people who had suffered need to hear that evil does not get the last word?

Verse 7 says "the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready." Verse 8 says her clothing was "given" to her, yet it is also "the righteous acts of the saints." Christians have long discussed how those two ideas fit together. What do you make of it?
When John falls at the angel's feet, the angel says, "Worship God!" (v. 10). What are some things, even good ones, that can quietly take the place of worship in our lives?
The rider is called "Faithful and True" and "The Word of God" (vv. 11, 13). If Jesus is Faithful and True, what difference does that make when you feel uncertain or let down?
The rider wears "a robe dipped in blood" before any battle begins (v. 13). Some readers see his enemies' blood, and others see his own blood shed on the cross. Which picture speaks to you, and why?
His only weapon is "a sharp sword" from His mouth (v. 15), and the armies behind Him are never shown fighting. What does that suggest about how Jesus wins?

Verses 17 to 21 are hard to read. Christians also differ on whether this describes a future event, a picture of how Jesus overcomes evil in every age, or something tied to Rome in John's day. What feelings come up for you when you read it, and what questions would you like to ask God about it?
19.life: Someone you know may be going through unfair treatment or suffering. This week, pray for them by name each day, asking God to bring justice and mercy. If you can, send them a short message to say you are thinking of them.
19.prayer: Praise God that "the Lord our God the Almighty reigns" (v. 6). Bring to him any situation where you long for justice, and ask him to help you trust him with it.
19.tip: Verses 17 to 21 are violent, and some people will be unsettled or even angry about them. Let them say so without hurrying to explain it away. Then point back to what the passage stresses: Jesus is Faithful and True, and evil is finally ended. Say plainly that Christians read the timing and imagery differently, and keep the focus on trusting his character.

20.open: When you were a kid, who was the person in charge whose fairness you trusted, like a teacher, coach or grandparent? What made you trust them?
questions: An angel binds "the dragon, that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan" (v. 2). Why might John want his readers to hear that evil has a limit and an end?
Verse 3 says Satan is sealed away "so that he could not deceive the nations." What does that tell us about the kind of harm he does? How have you seen deception hurt people?

Christians read the thousand years differently. Some expect a future reign of Christ on earth, others see Christ's reign now, and others expect a golden age before he returns. Which reading have you heard most, and what questions does it leave you with?

In verse 4, John sees those who were killed "for their testimony of Jesus" come to life and reign with Christ. What would these words have meant to believers who were being persecuted then? What might they mean for Christians who suffer today?
Verse 6 says "the second death has no power over them." What do you think it means to be safe from something like that? Where do you feel most in need of that kind of safety?
In verses 12 and 13 the dead, "great and small," all stand before the throne and are judged by the same standard. Does that feel more like a threat, a relief, or neither to you, and why?

Verse 15 is one of the Bible's hardest lines. Most churches have taught that it means endless punishment, some Christians read it as final destruction, and a few hope all will be restored. What stirs in you when you read it? Feel free to be honest if you are unsure or uneasy.
In verse 14 "Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire." What difference does it make to know that death itself does not get the last word?
20.life: Pick one person or situation that feels unfair or out of control right now. Each day this week, hand it to God in a sentence of prayer, trusting that he will one day make all things right.
20.prayer: Thank God that evil does not win and that death will not last forever. Ask for honesty about the questions this chapter raises, and for trust in a judge who is both fair and good.
20.tip: This chapter can pull the group into a debate about the thousand years or the fate of the lost. Say early and plainly that faithful Christians differ on both, and bring people back to what all agree on: Christ wins, evil ends, and God judges fairly. Leave room for anyone who is unsettled by verse 15 to say so without being corrected.

21.open: What is the best homecoming you have ever had, either coming home yourself or welcoming someone else?
questions: John sees "a new heaven and a new earth" (v. 1). When you picture the end of the story, what comes to mind first, and where do you think that picture comes from?
The voice says, "the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them" (v. 3). Why might God living with people be the heart of this vision rather than streets of gold?
Verse 4 promises that "He will wipe away every tear from their eyes." Which tears or losses would you most want to see wiped away, for yourself or for someone you love?

God says, "I make all things new" (v. 5), which is different from saying he makes a set of brand new things from scratch. What difference might that make for how we think about our lives and this world as they are now?
In verse 6 God offers water of life "freely" to the thirsty. What does it say about God that the invitation goes to the thirsty rather than the deserving? What are you thirsty for right now?

Verse 8 begins its list with "the cowardly" and ends with "all liars." Most Christians read the lake of fire as lasting punishment, and some understand it as final destruction. How do you honestly feel reading this verse, and what questions does it raise for you?
Verse 22 says there is no temple, "because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple." What would it mean for God's presence to be everywhere, with no special place needed to meet him?

Verse 24 says "the kings of the earth will bring their glory" into the city. What good things from human life and culture would you hope to see honored there? Feel free to say if parts of this vision feel hard to believe.
21.life: Pick one person you know who is grieving or worn out. This week, sit with them, send a note, or bring a meal, as a small sign of the day when God wipes away every tear.
21.prayer: Thank God that he chooses to live among his people. Ask him to meet the thirsty in your group and to comfort anyone carrying grief tonight.
21.tip: Verse 8 and the question of literal versus symbolic details (the cube, the jewels) can swallow the whole evening. Say plainly that Christians read these differently, give verse 8 a few honest minutes, then steer back to verses 3 and 4 and the promise that God makes his home with people.

22.open: What is a place you have been that felt like the best version of home, and what made it feel that way?
questions: John sees a river "as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (v. 1). What do you notice about the picture of God's presence here, and what does it make you feel?
Verse 2 says "the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations." Why do you think the Bible ends with healing? What would you most want to see healed?
Verse 3 says "No longer will there be any curse," and verse 4 says "They will see His face." This echoes the garden at the very start of the Bible. What do you think is being restored?
Twice John falls down to worship the angel, and is told, "Worship God!" (v. 9). Why is it so easy to give our deepest devotion to good things or good people that are not God?
Jesus says, "I am coming soon" (v. 12), and nearly two thousand years have passed. Christians read "soon" in different ways. How do you honestly feel about waiting, and what helps you keep hoping?
Verse 15 lists those who are outside the city, and verse 14 speaks of those who "wash their robes." How do you hear these verses: as a warning, a comfort, or something else? Be as honest as you like.
Verse 17 says, "let the one who is thirsty come, and the one who desires the water of life drink freely." What does it mean to you that the offer is free, and who comes to mind that needs to hear it?
The Bible ends with "Come, Lord Jesus" and "The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints" (vv. 20, 21). What does it say about the faith that it closes with a prayer and a blessing of grace?
22.life: Choose one thing in your life or in the world that is broken and that you long to see healed. Each day this week, pray for it briefly, ending with "Come, Lord Jesus." Then do one small, kind thing toward it.
22.prayer: Thank God that the story ends with him living openly with his people and with water offered freely to the thirsty. Ask him to keep our hope alive while we wait, and to bring healing to what hurts in us and around us.
22.tip: Verses 11, 15, 18 and 19 can sound harsh and may leave some people anxious about their standing with God. Read them in light of verses 14 and 17, where the robes are washed and the thirsty are invited to drink freely. Say plainly that Christians read the end of the book in different ways, and let anyone who is unsure speak without being corrected.
